Disgaea Mayhem Review

  • All Articles Headliners Reviews
  • Isaac Todd
  • September 7, 2026
  • 2
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:48
Instaread

When first revealed, Disgaea Mayhem seemed like it could be a decent side game to the long running SRPG franchise (Side note: Yes, I know it doesn’t include the Disgaea name in Japan.) You take the ridiculous attacks and stat grind of the main games and combine them with action combat, what could go wrong? Well, everything in Disgaea Mayhem‘s case.

Disgaea Mayhem sees you playing as the inexplicably named N.A., a mercenary hired by Overlord Tichelle to… recover some flan that was stolen. From the start it’s obvious that this isn’t supposed to be a serious story, at the cost of character development, memorable moments, or a coherent plot.

Humour is something present across the mainline games, but here it’s taken to the extreme. Worst part is that I don’t actually find it very funny, with story moments leaning mostly towards being stupid for the sake of it. Characters come and go, N.A. and Tichelle make some comments about flan, that’s about it.

You can essentially summarise the plot into a few lines without missing anything meaningful, and the main story already only takes a few hours to complete. There just nothing of substance, and not enough jokes land to even make up for that.

This lack of depth extends to combat itself. While you can recruit different monsters to follow you into each stage, you’re locked to playing as N.A. at all times. This takes away the usual fun of making your own characters in the main game, something I’d usually do as early as possible. He can at least make use of multiple weapons, though in practice that changes very little.

You see, Disgaea Mayhem gives you very little reason to care about which weapons you pick. They only have access to basic combos and up to four cooldown-based skills, none of which are particularly interesting. Most differences between weapons come in the form of some attacks being chargeable or extended by holding down that attack button. On its own this wouldn’t be unsalvageable, if paired up with some interesting level design.

This is where the game really commits its worst sin: levels are completely one-note. Each chapter of the main story is made up of one map, with each chapter taking place in one small section of it. Enemies spawn out of nowhere in small groups, replaced by another group when you defeat a certain amount. Repeat this a few times, take on a boss (most being a larger version of regular mobs) and you’re done in a few minutes.

Despite looking like Koei Tecmo’s Warriors franchise on the surface, Disgaea Mayhem doesn’t really understand what makes those work. You need unique stages with thought out level design, and mid-mission events that force you to quickly move across the battlefield. None of that is here. Instead, it barely evolves past mindless button mashing across a small handful of areas.

Making things worse is just how ugly the game looks most of the time. Environments are barren, animations are often lacking flair, and there’s never the grand scale of even the PS2 Dynasty Warriors titles. On top of this, the Switch 2 version of Disgaea Mayhem is especially poor, featuring an inconsistent framerate and and blurry visuals outside of cutscenes.

The only area that sees any amount of success is grinding, funnily enough. You have access to the usual things, including a 9999 level cap, reincarnation to reset your levels for a stat boost, and the item world for strengthening weapons. In the endgame you also start collecting weapons that give permanent stats when upgraded via the item world, even if you’re not using them.

My problem with this is that the gameplay loop just isn’t that fun. Efficient grinding in the mainline Disgaea games isn’t too bad since you can speed up gameplay and skip animations. Here, you’re forced to mash away through identical waves of enemies with no way to make things faster. A least the pace of experience gains is increased, with N.A.’s level well into the thousands for me before I’d even hit 10 hours played.

Disgaea Mayhem Review – Final Thoughts

Disgaea Mayhem is an incredibly rough first draft of a concept that has potential. But I’d have a hard time recommending it at over half its current price, let alone £49.99+. Even if you’re fine with the difference in genre, this isn’t worth picking up even for diehard Disgaea fans.

Disgaea Mayhem was reviewed on Switch 2 using a code provided by the publisher.
